description_full: CDW Corporation provides information technology (IT) solutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. It operates through three segments: Commercial, Government, and Education. The company offers discrete hardware and software products and services, as well as integrated IT solutions, including on-premise and cloud capabilities across hybrid infrastructure, digital experience, and security. It also provides hardware products comprising notebooks/mobile devices, tablets, network communications, collaboration hardware, data storage and servers, desktop computers, and other hardware; and software products, such as cloud solutions, software assurance, application suites, security, virtualization, collaboration and productivity applications, operating systems, and network management. In addition, the company offers advisory and design, software development, implementation, and managed services, as well as warranties. It serves business, government, education, and healthcare customers. The company was formerly known as CDW Computer Centers, Inc. and changed its name to CDW Corporation in June 2003. CDW Corporation was founded in 1984 and is based in Vernon Hills, Illinois.
ceo_bio: Ms. Christine A. Leahy J.D. | Chair of the Board, President & CEO | Age 60 | Compensation: $3.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 14K people. Revenue per employee of $1.5M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $74K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: CDW Corporation is a large-cap technology business with a $19.6B market cap on $22.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 8% cost of capital, a 10-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.13× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 7.1×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
